title: Lost confidence: replacing RICE-style confidence scores with decisions that work under uncertainty
summary: Jason Cohen argues that confidence scores in frameworks like RICE are noise: undefined, untrustworthy, and they bias prioritization toward small safe projects. He proposes uncertainty-proof techniques instead: bet on what is always true, validate with behavior, measure impact, invest in leverage, maximize optionality, and choose between portfolios and asymmetric bets.

principles.text: Confidence scores in prioritization frameworks systematically favor small safe projects over large high-value ones.
principles.quote: we're typically confident in small projects and unconfident in larger projects, as well we should be. But that systematically skews the prioritization away from delivering as much value as possible

principles.text: Even experienced PMs are regularly certain about features that flop, so stated confidence is not reliable evidence.
principles.quote: Can you recall a feature you were *certain* would be well-received, but wasn't?

principles.text: Invest in things that are true under any circumstance, like speed, rather than estimating user interest percentages.
principles.quote: identify the features where essentially all customers will either value them, or at least enjoy them.

principles.text: Test demand with behavior, such as dummy-feature buttons, not hypothetical survey answers.
Define high impact concretely: used by a majority, or cited as a top-three reason by a passionate minority.
principles.quote: A high-impact feature is either (1) regularly used by at least 51% of customers, or (2) cited by at least 15% of customers in their top three reasons for choosing or retaining your product.

principles.text: Use portfolios for reliable incremental results; use asymmetric bets with time-boxed, bounded downside to hunt outliers.
principles.quote: If the worst case is "we lose two months" and the best case is "we're completely differentiated," the probability barely matters.
